# Class 9 chemistry, ~2 minutes, written by Claude for F-014 S3 (processes). Expect: a content slide on the structure
# of the atom; Rutherford's "circular orbits" is not the Bohr model (test4 trap); "let me show you the Bohr model"
# opens simulation mode (nucleus, four empty shells, no electrons); "sodium, atomic number 11" fills 2, 8, 1 (valence 1);
# "iron" is not used (Z > 20, a notice); orbitals get a notice; hydrogen's electron falling from the third level to the
# second emits a photon of 1.89 eV, 656 nm; "let's get back to the slides" ends the mode with a recap; then valency.
@setup subject=Chemistry grade=9 topic="Structure of the atom"

Good morning everyone. Today we continue with the structure of the atom.
[pause 1]
Rutherford said that electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits, but his model could not explain why the atom is stable.
Niels Bohr improved this model in 1913.
[pause 1.5]
Let me show you the Bohr model of the atom.
At the centre is the nucleus, which has protons and neutrons.
The electrons revolve in fixed shells called K, L, M and N, and each shell can hold a fixed number of electrons.
[pause 1]
Take sodium, atomic number 11.
Its electrons are arranged as 2, 8 and 1, so it has one valence electron.
Iron has many more electrons, but we will not draw it today.
In higher classes you will learn about orbitals like 1s and 2p.
[pause 1]
Now take hydrogen.
When its electron absorbs energy, it gets excited and jumps to a higher shell.
When the electron falls from the third level to the second, it emits a photon of red light.
[pause 1.5]
Okay, let's get back to the slides.
[pause 1]
The electrons in the outermost shell are called valence electrons.
The number of valence electrons decides how an atom combines with other atoms. This is called valency.
